body:
A distinctive regional development in Karnataka

The Hoysala dynasty patronised a distinctive school of temple architecture in Karnataka, particularly during the 12th and 13th centuries CE. Its buildings developed in the wider Deccan environment, where different northern and southern architectural ideas had long interacted.

Hoysala temples are sometimes included in discussions of Vesara or hybrid Deccan architecture. However, they also have a sufficiently distinctive combination of features to be recognised as a separate regional school.

The stellate or star-shaped plan

One of the most important Hoysala features is the stellate plan. Stellate means star-shaped. Instead of forming a simple square outline, the outer walls and supporting platform are arranged through multiple angular projections and recesses.

These repeated projections give the temple a star-like appearance when seen from above. They also create numerous wall surfaces for sculpture. The architectural plan and decorative programme are therefore closely related.

Not every Hoysala shrine has exactly the same number of projections, and the star-shaped plan should not be confused with a circular plan. The principal idea is the multiplication of angles around the shrine.

Materials and carved decoration

Hoysala monuments commonly use chloritic schist, often described as soapstone. Its relatively workable character allowed sculptors to produce delicate surface details.

Typical features include densely carved wall panels, ornamental bands running around the base and carefully executed details of figures, jewellery, animals and architectural motifs. The platform often follows the projecting outline of the temple itself.

The external surface therefore appears very different from the smoother, more strongly vertical presentation of many earlier temples. The Hoysala emphasis is not only on tower height but also on the richly articulated plan and sculptural walls.

Three major Hoysala temple examples

TemplePlacePrincipal dedication
Chennakeshava TempleBelur, KarnatakaVishnu
Hoysalesvara TempleHalebidu, KarnatakaShiva
Keshava TempleSomanathapura, KarnatakaVishnu

The Chennakeshava Temple at Belur is a major early expression of the mature Hoysala school. The Hoysalesvara Temple at Halebidu is notable for its double-shrine arrangement and extensive carved decoration. The Keshava Temple at Somanathapura is an important later example of the developed Hoysala approach.

These 3 monuments form the UNESCO-listed Sacred Ensembles of the Hoysalas. Their common architectural vocabulary makes the group especially useful for comparing examples from different places within the same regional tradition.

Why Hoysala temples must not be reduced to a simple hybrid label

The Hoysala school drew upon existing temple architecture but created its own recognisable arrangements of plans, surfaces and decorative details. Consequently, a comparison question may identify a Hoysala temple from its stellate base and elaborate stone carving even when its surviving tower is incomplete.

Some important Hoysala towers have been lost. Their absence today does not erase the architectural evidence provided by the surviving plan, platform and sculptural treatment.

Prelims focus

  • Hoysala architecture developed prominently in Karnataka during the 12th–13th centuries CE.
  • Stellate means star-shaped and refers to an angular temple plan.
  • Soapstone or chloritic schist enabled intricate carving.
  • Belur: Chennakeshava Temple; Halebidu: Hoysalesvara Temple; Somanathapura: Keshava Temple.
  • Hoysala buildings form a distinctive regional school within the broader Deccan architectural setting.
  • Trap: Stellate means a projecting angular plan, not simply a tall curved shikhara.

[NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Class 11, Chapter 6, Temple Architecture and Sculpture, printed pp. 88–89; UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Sacred Ensembles of the Hoysalas, Outstanding Universal Value, Brief Synthesis and Description (consulted 23 November 2026).]

body:
The western Indian architectural tradition

The temple-building tradition of Gujarat and neighbouring Rajasthan developed important regional features within the wider Nagara architectural world. A major style associated with this region is known as Maru-Gurjara, also frequently called the Solanki style.

The term Maru-Gurjara refers to the architectural relationship between western Indian regions, especially Rajasthan and Gujarat. The style became prominent under the Chaulukya or Solanki rulers, particularly from the 10th to the 13th centuries CE.

Its identifying characteristics include richly articulated walls, projecting architectural surfaces, decorative columns, elaborately carved ceilings, ornamental gateways and a carefully organised relationship between the sanctum and assembly halls. These elements could appear in both Hindu and Jain temples.

Maru-Gurjara should not be treated as the southern Dravida order merely because some of its halls have elaborate ceilings or stepped elements. It is a distinctive western Indian regional tradition with strong Nagara associations.

Modhera: location, patronage and dedication

The Sun Temple at Modhera stands in the Mehsana district of Gujarat, near the Pushpavati River. It is dedicated to Surya.

The temple belongs to the early 11th century CE. Gujarat Tourism, referring to the Archaeological Survey of India, dates its construction to 1026–1027 CE, during the reign of Bhima I of the Chaulukya or Solanki dynasty.

The arrangement of the temple is particularly important because the sacred building is approached through a sequence of spaces closely related to a large stepped water tank.

The main architectural components of Modhera

The principal elements are:

  • Surya Kund: A large rectangular stepped tank situated in front of the temple. Its steps incorporate 108 smaller shrines.
  • Torana: An ornamental arched gateway associated with the approach towards the assembly hall.
  • Sabha Mandapa: An elaborate pillared assembly hall, open on its sides, located between the kund and the principal shrine structure.
  • Gudhamandapa: The enclosed or covered hall associated with the main shrine.
  • Garbhagriha: The innermost sanctum of the principal temple.

The arrangement connects water, movement and sacred architecture along a common approach. The large kund is not merely a small decorative basin. It forms a substantial architectural component of the Modhera complex.

Sunlight and the temple's eastward orientation

The temple was planned with an eastward orientation. Historical descriptions associate this alignment with the ability of the rising sun's rays, particularly at the equinoxes, to pass towards the principal sanctum.

The equinoxes occur around March and September, when day and night are approximately equal in duration. The architectural significance here is the intentional relationship between the temple's orientation and the sun's position.

The original tall superstructure above the main shrine no longer survives. The present complex should therefore be studied through its surviving halls, platform, carvings and stepped tank rather than through an imagined intact original shikhara.

Other Gujarat examples of the same regional tradition

Maru-Gurjara architecture was not restricted to Sun temples. Important examples of its broader development include:

  • Ajitanatha Jain Temple at Taranga: A major Jain monument in the Mehsana region, associated with the Solanki period.
  • Rudra Mahalaya at Siddhpur: An important historical temple complex associated with the Chaulukya architectural tradition.
  • Jain temples at Kumbhariya: Examples of richly developed western Indian temple architecture.

These examples show that the regional architectural vocabulary could be used across different religious traditions. The main identifying relationship is architectural and geographical, not exclusive dedication to a single deity or community.

Modhera and Konark must be distinguished

FeatureModheraKonark
StateGujaratOdisha
Architectural traditionMaru-GurjaraKalinga
PeriodEarly 11th century CE13th century CE
Dynastic patronageChaulukya or Solanki; Bhima IEastern Ganga; Narasimhadeva I
Principal visual clueStepped Surya Kund and elaborate pillared hallsStone chariot with 24 wheels

Both temples are dedicated to Surya, but their periods, patrons, regional styles and characteristic architectural features differ.

Prelims focus

  • Maru-Gurjara is a western Indian temple style associated particularly with Gujarat and Rajasthan.
  • Modhera Sun Temple: Mehsana district, Gujarat; Surya dedication.
  • Patronage: Bhima I of the Chaulukya or Solanki dynasty; 1026–1027 CE.
  • Surya Kund: large rectangular stepped tank containing 108 smaller shrines.
  • Other Gujarat examples include Taranga, Siddhpur and Kumbhariya.
  • Trap: Modhera's stepped kund is different from Konark's 24 carved chariot wheels.

[NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Class 11, Chapter 6, Temple Architecture and Sculpture, printed pp. 75–76; Gujarat Tourism, Modhera Sun Temple, Brief History and site description (consulted 23 November 2026); UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Sun Temple, Modhera and its adjoining monuments, India's Tentative List submission dated 13 December 2022, Description (consulted 23 November 2026); UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Sacred Ensembles of the Hoysalas, nomination documentation, section 2, Solanki or Maru-Gurjara Temples (consulted 23 November 2026).]

title: Gujarat's Maru-Gurjara Style and the Sun Temple at Modhera

body:
The correct method of architectural identification

Indian temple architecture is best understood through the relationship between plan, elevation, region and historical patronage. A temple should not be classified merely because it contains a tall tower, a stepped roof or an elaborate gateway.

The 2 principal broad orders are Nagara and Dravida. Vesara is commonly used for important hybrid developments in the Deccan. Within these larger classifications, regional schools such as Kalinga, Maru-Gurjara and Hoysala developed distinctive combinations of architectural features.

Comparison of the major styles and regional schools

Style or schoolPrincipal clueRegionRecognisable example
NagaraFrequently a curving shikhara above the sanctumNorthern IndiaKhajuraho temples
DravidaStepped pyramidal vimana; developed enclosure and gopuram traditionsSouthern IndiaBrihadisvara, Thanjavur
VesaraInteraction of northern and southern forms; no single compulsory tower shapeDeccanChalukya architectural experiments
KalingaRekha deul and stepped pidha roof over the jagamohanaOdishaKonark Sun Temple
Maru-GurjaraRichly carved western Indian temples, halls and ornamental detailsGujarat and RajasthanModhera Sun Temple
HoysalaStellate plan and dense carving in soapstoneKarnatakaBelur, Halebidu and Somanathapura temples

The table identifies each style by its most useful introductory clue. The categories are not all mutually exclusive. For example, Kalinga and Maru-Gurjara are regional developments within the broader northern architectural tradition, while Hoysala architecture developed within the wider environment of Deccan architectural exchange.

Names, periods and patrons that must be matched correctly

MonumentDynasty or patronPeriod
Deogarh Vishnu TempleLate Gupta-period architectural traditionEarly 6th century CE
Lakshmana Temple, KhajurahoChandela ruler YashovarmanApproximately 954 CE
Shore Temple, MamallapuramPallava ruler Narasimhavarman IIEarly 8th century CE
Virupaksha Temple, PattadakalQueen Lokamahadevi; reign of Vikramaditya IIApproximately 740 CE
Kailasa Temple, ElloraRashtrakuta ruler Krishna I8th century CE
Brihadisvara, ThanjavurChola ruler Rajaraja I1009–1010 CE
Modhera Sun TempleChaulukya ruler Bhima I1026–1027 CE
Konark Sun TempleEastern Ganga ruler Narasimhadeva I13th century CE

Five distinctions that prevent common errors

  • Sanctum versus entrance: The garbhagriha houses the principal deity. A gopuram marks an entrance through an enclosure wall.
  • Temple tower versus hall roof: A Nagara sanctum may have a latina shikhara while its mandapa has a phamsana roof. An Odisha temple may combine a rekha deul with a pidha-roofed jagamohana.
  • Religious dedication versus architectural style: The Sun temples at Modhera and Konark share a dedication but belong to different regional schools.
  • Construction method versus style: Ellora's Kailasa Temple is monolithic and architecturally Dravida. Monolithic is not another name for Vesara.
  • Broad order versus regional school: Nagara and Dravida are broad classifications; Kalinga, Maru-Gurjara and Hoysala identify important regional developments.

Applying the distinctions to architectural evidence

Suppose the surviving structure has a large stepped assembly-hall roof, but the site is in Odisha and the historical main shrine had a curving deul. The correct interpretation is a Kalinga arrangement within the Nagara tradition, not a Dravida temple merely because one roof is pyramidal.

Similarly, if a Karnataka temple has an angular star-shaped base and unusually intricate soapstone carvings, the combined evidence strongly suggests the Hoysala school. A single curved tower or a single stone carving would be much weaker evidence.

If a temple photograph shows a rectangular stepped tank in front of elaborate halls, the distinguishing facts of Modhera should be considered. If the monument is conceived as a stone chariot with 24 wheels, the association is Konark.

A reliable identification sequence

First locate the garbhagriha and identify the tower above it. Next examine the mandapa, gateways and enclosure. Then consider the temple's plan and characteristic regional details. Finally, confirm the place, dynasty, period and dedication.

Prelims focus

  • Nagara: northern architectural order; curving shikhara is a common clue.
  • Dravida: southern architectural order; stepped vimana and gopuram are important clues.
  • Vesara: hybrid architectural developments associated with the Deccan.
  • Kalinga: Odisha; Maru-Gurjara: Gujarat and Rajasthan; Hoysala: Karnataka.
  • Brihadisvara–Rajaraja I; Khajuraho–Chandelas; Konark–Narasimhadeva I; Modhera–Bhima I.
  • Trap: Shared features and shared religious dedications do not make 2 temples members of the same regional school.

[NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Class 11, Chapter 6, Temple Architecture and Sculpture, printed pp. 69–89; Archaeological Survey of India, Group of Temples, Khajuraho, and Ellora Caves, monument descriptions (consulted 23 November 2026); UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Group of Monuments at Pattadakal, Great Living Chola Temples, Sun Temple at Konark, and Sacred Ensembles of the Hoysalas, respective property descriptions and Outstanding Universal Value statements (consulted 23 November 2026); Gujarat Tourism, Modhera Sun Temple, Brief History (consulted 23 November 2026).]
